t.yukon river crossing@65.9,-149.7:
Few bridges feel as lonely as the one over the Yukon River on the Dalton Highway. It is a long steel truss with a wooden deck, completed in the mid-1970s to carry the trucks that built the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, and the pipeline itself runs alongside, a silver snake sliding across the river on its own supports. Fairbanks lies a long day behind, and the Arctic lies ahead. At this point the highway has already left pavement and certainty well behind.

The road here is part of a gravel highway about four hundred miles long, rough and dusty or slippery with mud depending on the weather. It was built as a haul road for the pipeline and still carries heavy trucks at all hours, which throw stones, raise dust, and take their share of the road without apology. Riders give them room and keep lights on, slow in the dust and pull over well clear when one approaches. The grades on the approach to the bridge are steep, and the deck itself can be slick when wet, so ride slowly and keep off the edges.

Beside the river there is a small camp offering fuel, basic food and rooms, which is a big deal in a country where services are separated by many hours. Fuel is not casual up here: the next dependable pumps beyond are at Coldfoot, a long way north, so top up whenever you can. Mosquitoes in summer are ferocious, and weather can swing from hot sun to cold rain in an afternoon. A dry bag, spare tubes, tools and extra water are not optional.

The Yukon itself is a huge, brown, powerful river, one of the great waterways of North America, and standing at the bridge you feel its weight. Boreal forest of black spruce and birch stretches in all directions, and the light in the long northern summer evenings is almost endless. Travel here is an adventure as much as a ride; go prepared, go slowly, and tell someone your plan.
t.atigun pass@68.1,-149.5:
The Atigun Pass is the highest road pass in Alaska, 1,444 metres above sea level, and it carries the Dalton Highway through the Brooks Range, the last great barrier before the North Slope and the Arctic Ocean. The mountains here are bare, with jagged grey rock and green tundra, and the continental divide runs across the top, so that rivers on one side flow to the Pacific and Arctic waters on the other. The trans-Alaska pipeline climbs beside the road, running above the ground on steel supports so that its heat will not thaw the permafrost, and it is both a marvel of engineering and a reminder of how remote this country is.

The Dalton Highway was built in 1974 as a haul road for the pipeline, and it remains a working road, with heavy trucks hauling supplies north to the oil fields at Prudhoe Bay. It is more than 400 miles long and mostly gravel, and it is not a road for casual riders. The surface can be loose, rutted and slick when wet, and in summer the road is often treated with calcium chloride to control the dust, which turns to a greasy mud and coats the bike. Stone chips fly from passing trucks, which have right of way, so ride defensively and move over for them.

Atigun's steep grades and tight bends demand attention, and snow can fall any month of the year, so carry warm layers and waterproofs. The wildlife is a bonus. Dall sheep graze on the slopes, caribou cross the tundra, and musk oxen may be seen north of the pass. Mosquitoes in July are fierce, and a head net is a good idea. In summer, the sun scarcely sets, and the landscape glows in a soft light at midnight.

The nearest is Coldfoot, about seventy miles south, which has fuel, food and a basic lodge, and the next fuel to the north is at Deadhorse, roughly a hundred and seventy miles beyond the pass. Carry spare fuel, tools, a spare tyre or repair kit and a satellite messenger, as there is little phone coverage. It is a serious ride, and a rewarding one.
t.divnogorsk@56.0,92.4:
Divnogorsk is a company town that turned into a proper one. It grew from the late 1950s around the Krasnoyarsk Dam, a huge concrete hydropower station on the Yenisei that for years ranked among the largest in the world, and today around thirty thousand people live in tidy streets squeezed between the river and the steep, forested slopes of the Sayan foothills. The name means something like a place of wonders, and while that is generous for a Soviet-era dam town, the setting earns it: the Yenisei here is wide, cold and fast, coming out of the reservoir like a gate has been opened.

The road from Krasnoyarsk upstream along the river is a pleasure for any rider who enjoys a bit of rhythm. The highway climbs and falls through spruce and birch, curling beside the water, with a good surface in most places and enough bends to keep you busy without wearing you out. Traffic can be heavy near the city, thinning as you head south, and in winter this stretch can be icy in the shaded corners, so late spring through early autumn is the sensible window. Early mornings, with mist over the river, are the best time of day.

With around thirty thousand residents, Divnogorsk has all the services you might need: fuel, cafes, supermarkets and a handful of hotels. It also has a viewpoint over the dam, and an old ship lift built to carry vessels past the wall, though it is no longer in regular use. A short ride away, the village of Ovsyanka is the birthplace of the writer Viktor Astafiev, one of the best-loved voices of late Soviet literature, and a small museum there tells his story, with the Yenisei and the taiga as the backdrop to his books.

The river deserves a moment. The Yenisei is one of the great rivers of Siberia, flowing north for thousands of kilometres to the Arctic, and here it is still young and clear, fed by the mountains. The dam has changed its flow and temperature, so that in some winters the water below the wall stays open and steams in the frost. Bring a layer, because the air near the water is colder than you expect, and enjoy the sense of riding beside something much bigger than a road.
t.golmud@36.4,94.9:
Golmud is a city built on a salt flat, and it exists because of the road. The name comes from a Mongolian word for river, which sounds optimistic for a place on the edge of the Qaidam Basin, a vast, high desert of salt lakes, gravel plains and oil wells. At about 2,800 metres, with the Kunlun mountains rising to the south, it is a modern, wide-avenued city of several hundred thousand people that grew from almost nothing in the 1950s, when engineers began pushing a highway and later a railway across the Tibetan plateau.

This is the staging post for the Qinghai-Tibet Highway, the road that climbs from here over the Kunlun Pass, at well over 4,700 metres, and runs across the Tibetan plateau toward Lhasa, more than a thousand kilometres away. The railway to Lhasa, opened in 2006, was one of the most ambitious pieces of engineering of its time, laid partly on permafrost with cooling systems to keep the ground from thawing. The road runs alongside it in places, with herds of Tibetan antelope, wild yaks and kiang visible on the grasslands in the high country, and prayer flags marking passes.

The riding is of a kind that few ever experience. The road is mostly paved and busy with trucks, but the altitude is the real challenge, with long climbs to over five thousand metres, thin air, bitter cold even in summer and sudden snow. Engines lose power, riders lose concentration, and acute mountain sickness is a real danger on a rapid ascent. The plateau is vast and bare, with a sky of intense blue and clouds that throw long shadows across the ranges.

An honest note on access: foreign visitors generally cannot ride independently here. Tibet requires special permits and guided travel, and riding in China requires a Chinese licence and registration, so for most travellers this road is something to read about or to see from a train window. If you do plan any trip in the region, check current rules with an agency before committing.

Golmud itself has all the practical services of a regional city, including fuel, hotels, restaurants and workshops. Nearby salt lakes, including Qarhan, yield potash and other minerals, and the flat, glittering plains around them are some of the most surreal landscapes in China. The best months are usually late spring and early autumn, while winter closes parts of the high plateau with ice and snow.
t.krasnoyarsk@56.0,92.9:
Krasnoyarsk is a proper city, a million people strong, spread along the Yenisei where the great river leaves the Sayan foothills and begins its journey north to the Arctic. Anton Chekhov, passing through in 1890, described it as the most beautiful city in Siberia, and while locals love quoting that, you can see what he meant when you ride along the embankment on a clear evening. Solnechny, a suburb, lies a few kilometres away, and the Trans-Siberian crosses the river on a long bridge in the city centre.

As a stop it is excellent. There is fuel everywhere, mechanics, bike shops, restaurants and hotels, and the road network is solid, so this is the place to sort out any problems. Riding into the city from the west is a slog through suburban traffic, but the Yenisei itself is worth the effort. The ride toward Divnogorsk goes along the river, with hills and forest on both sides, and the road is one of the more enjoyable around the city: long bends, decent surface and views down to the water. Early morning or weekdays are best, since weekends bring heavy traffic.

The city's history begins in 1628, when Cossacks built a wooden fort here, and it later became a trading town on the road to the east. The Soviet period brought heavy industry, aluminium and, during the Second World War, evacuated factories, and the city grew rapidly. Nearby, the Krasnoyarsk hydroelectric dam, finished in the early 1970s, holds back a huge reservoir and has an odd effect: the river below the dam stays open in winter, with steam rising from the water in the frost. A ship lift beside the dam is a notable piece of engineering.

The nature around Krasnoyarsk is the best part. Just upriver lies the Stolby nature reserve, a forested area dotted with granite pillars that climbers have scaled since the nineteenth century and that locals treat as a near-sacred playground. Pine and birch forest covers the hills, and on warm days the smell of resin mixes with river air. Bears, elk and sable live in the reserve, though you will not meet them on the road.

The city has plenty of places to eat, and it is easy to find a quiet corner by the water. Fill the tank here and leave early to enjoy the road toward Divnogorsk.
